clinician.final_diagnosis: Carcinomatous meningitis secondary to non-small cell lung adenocarcinoma
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 76-year-old male smoker presented with a 2-month progressive meningeal syndrome characterized by headache, nausea, vomiting, intermittent fever, and cervical rigidity. Initial CSF analysis revealed elevated pressure (220 mmH2O), elevated protein (0.76 g/L), pleocytosis (6 × 10^6 cells/L with mononuclear predominance), and normal glucose/chlorides. Initial CSF cytology was negative for atypical cells. Brain MRI showed only lacunar infarctions in the basal ganglia without documented leptomeningeal enhancement. Repeat CSF cytology subsequently identified malignant cells with enlarged nuclei, increased nucleocytoplasmic ratios, and hyperchromatic features. Systemic investigation revealed sputum cytology positive for adenocarcinoma cells, and chest CT identified a nodule in the right upper lobe. Non-small cell lung cancer was diagnosed at stage IVB (T1bN2M1c). The patient was treated with whole brain radiotherapy and intrathecal methotrexate (weekly for the first month, then monthly). Clinical symptoms (headache and vomiting) resolved after three months of treatment.
